name: Koop / CTS Ultra

citations.title: KoopCast podcast and CTS Ultra coaching

description: Ultra-specific system from CTS coach Jason Koop, built around the principles that ultras are won by being durable, not fast. Heart rate-anchored zones, back-to-back long runs on weekends, vertical gain progression, and explicit terrain specificity. Covers 50K through 100-mile races including mountain ultras.
signature: Back-to-back long runs on weekends, terrain-specific training, and HR-zone-based intensity prescription
philosophyNarrative: Koop's CTS Ultra system rejects the road-marathon training mindset. For ultras, Koop argues, fitness matters less than durability: your ability to keep moving when fueling fails, terrain punishes you, and the day stretches past 12 hours. Five principles drive the system: (1) heart rate trumps pace — paces vary wildly with terrain and fatigue, so HR is the only consistent metric; (2) back-to-back long runs (Saturday + Sunday) build the cumulative time-on-feet that defines ultra-readiness; (3) vertical gain is its own training stress — plans target weekly elevation specific to the goal race; (4) terrain specificity matters more than intensity prescription — train on the surfaces you'll race on; (5) durability work (steep hikes, descending) is non-optional for mountain ultras. Plans range 16-32 weeks depending on distance and goal. Koop uses Endurance, Tempo, SteadyState, and ClimbingRepeats as primary workouts.

paceZones.purpose: Active recovery between long efforts. HR <80% LTHR.
Aerobic base — bulk of weekly volume and most of the long-run time. HR 80-90% LTHR. Slow on uphills, faster on flats.
Sustained aerobic intensity — Koop's 'Tempo' is essentially extended aerobic threshold work. HR 90-95% LTHR. 30-60 min continuous.

rpeRange.description: Comfortably hard; sustainable for an hour

paceZones.purpose: Lactate threshold work. HR 95-100% LTHR. Used in interval format (3-15 min reps) or continuous (15-30 min). Critical for shorter ultras (50K-50M).
VO2max-equivalent intensity, typically performed on uphill terrain. 2-5 min hill repeats. HR 100-105% LTHR. Used sparingly — durability matters more than VO2 ceiling for ultras.

rpeRange.description: Hard; on uphills, this is climbing effort

workouts.name: Endurance Run (Z2)
workouts.shortDescription: Aerobic run at Zone 2 — the bulk of weekly volume

mainSet.cue: Hold Zone 2. On hills, pace will slow but HR stays in zone — slow down or hike if needed.

workouts.purpose: Aerobic base building. Most weekly volume is here. On trails, expect to hike steep climbs to maintain Z2 — this is correct.
cues: Slow down or hike on climbs to keep HR in Z2
Pace varies wildly with terrain — HR is the constant
Bulk of long runs are at this intensity

workouts.name: Back-to-Back Long Runs
workouts.shortDescription: Saturday long + Sunday long — Koop's signature ultra preparation

mainSet.description: Sat: long run at Endurance pace; Sun: medium-long run at Endurance pace
mainSet.cue: The Saturday long run is your hardest workout of the week. Sunday's long run starts with tired legs — that's the point. This pair builds ultra-specific durability.

workouts.purpose: The CTS Ultra signature workout. Saturday long run + Sunday medium-long run trains time-on-feet under pre-existing fatigue — the central physiological demand of ultras. Used 2-3× per month in the specific-prep phase.
cues: Saturday: target race-distance practice (longer for shorter races)
Sunday: 50-70% of Saturday's duration; HR may drift higher at same pace
Practice race-day fueling on both days
Hike steep terrain to keep HR in zone — running every step is not the goal

workouts.name: Long Run (single)
workouts.shortDescription: Single weekly long run for 50K-distance plans or recovery weeks

mainSet.description: Long steady run at Endurance pace
mainSet.cue: Cumulative time on feet. For mountain ultras, target similar elevation gain to your race. Hike steep terrain.

workouts.purpose: Endurance and time-on-feet. Single long runs are the default in base phase; back-to-backs replace them in specific prep.
cues: Time on feet matters more than mileage
On trails, target similar vertical to your goal race
Practice race-day fueling and gear (vest, poles, headlamp for night portions)

workouts.name: Tempo (Z3)
workouts.shortDescription: 30-60 min continuous at aerobic threshold (Z3) — extended sustainable effort

mainSet.cue: Sustainable aerobic effort. Pace varies with terrain — HR is the gauge.

workouts.purpose: Aerobic threshold development — the intensity at which you'll spend significant time during ultras. Extended sustainable effort is more race-specific than VO2max work for ultras.
cues: Steady HR throughout — even if pace drops
On trails, run flats and downhills, hike steep climbs
Build duration across the program: 30 → 45 → 60 min

workouts.name: SteadyState Intervals (Z4)
workouts.shortDescription: Lactate threshold intervals — 3-15 min reps at Z4

mainSet.cue: Threshold effort. Hold Z4 for the full duration of each rep.

workouts.purpose: Lactate threshold development. Especially important for 50K-50M races where intensity matters more than for 100M+. Used in the specific-prep phase.
cues: Even effort across all reps
If reps slow significantly, end the workout
On trails, choose rolling/runnable terrain

workouts.name: Climbing Repeats (Z5)
workouts.shortDescription: Hill repeats at high intensity — develops climbing-specific strength

warmup.description: Easy run to base of hill

mainSet.cue: Climb at Zone 5 effort. Choose a hill steep enough that HR rises naturally — let the grade do the work.

workouts.purpose: Develops climbing-specific strength and VO2max. Especially valuable for mountain ultras. Replaces flat speedwork in CTS Ultra plans.
cues: Choose a hill ~6-10% grade
Effort, not pace — let the grade work for you
Walk down for recovery; reset for next rep

workouts.name: Durability Hike
workouts.shortDescription: Steep uphill hiking session — builds vertical gain capacity

mainSet.description: Steady uphill hiking on steep terrain
mainSet.cue: Hike at sustainable Z2 effort on steep terrain (>10% grade). Use poles if you'll race with them. Builds vertical gain capacity without running impact.

workouts.purpose: Builds vertical gain capacity and hiking-specific strength for mountain ultras. Lower impact than running, allows more total vertical per week.
cues: Hike, don't run — stay in Z2 even on the steepest sections
Practice with poles if you'll race with them
Target similar vertical-gain rate to your goal race

workouts.name: Recovery Run
workouts.shortDescription: Very easy short run between hard efforts

mainSet.cue: HR strictly Z1 (<80% LTHR). The point is movement, not training.

workouts.purpose: Active recovery between hard sessions and after back-to-back long runs.
cues: Walk if HR drifts up
Skip if genuinely depleted

phases.name: Base
phases.focus: Build aerobic base. Single long runs (no back-to-backs yet). Tempo work begins. Vertical gain progression.
phases.athleteNarrative: Welcome to CTS Ultra Base phase. Your priority here is aerobic base and weekly vertical gain. Most weekly running is at Zone 2 (Endurance). One Tempo session per week. For mountain ultras, durability hikes build vertical capacity without running impact. Single long runs on Sunday — back-to-backs come in the next phase. Trust the volume — for ultras, time-on-feet is everything.

phases.name: Specific Prep
phases.focus: Back-to-back long runs introduced. SteadyState intervals. ClimbingRepeats for mountain ultras. Race-specific terrain and gear practice.
phases.athleteNarrative: Specific Prep phase. The back-to-back long run is now your most important workout — Saturday's long run is followed by Sunday's medium-long run. This trains the cumulative fatigue that defines ultras. SteadyState intervals build threshold for shorter ultras; ClimbingRepeats build climbing strength for mountain races. Practice race gear (vest, poles, headlamp) and race fueling on the back-to-backs.

phases.name: Race Prep
phases.focus: Peak back-to-backs (longest of the program). Final ClimbingRepeats. Begin taper end of phase.
phases.athleteNarrative: Race Prep. Peak back-to-back long runs occur here — the longest two-day blocks in the program. For 100-milers, peak might be 35 mi Saturday + 25 mi Sunday. Final ClimbingRepeats sharpen climbing strength. After this phase, taper begins. The work is being banked.

phases.name: Taper
phases.focus: Reduce volume sharply. Light vertical gain to maintain hiking adaptation. Final shake-out.
phases.athleteNarrative: Taper. CTS Ultra taper is longer than for road races — typically 3-4 weeks for 100-milers, 2-3 for 50-milers. Volume drops, but light vertical gain (1-2 short hikes) maintains your hiking adaptation. Sleep, hydrate, plan logistics. The work is done.

weeklyPatterns.notes: Base 5-day. Single long run Sunday. Tempo Tuesday. Optional durability hike Thursday for mountain runners.

schedule.notes: B2B Day 2 (Sun) — medium-long run on tired legs

weeklyPatterns.notes: Specific prep 6-day. Tuesday SteadyState + Thursday ClimbingRepeats + B2B long runs on Sat/Sun. Most demanding pattern.
5-day specific prep. Drops the recovery run to keep B2B intact.
Race prep peak. Longest B2B of the program. After this, taper begins.

schedule.notes: Cutback long run — single, no B2B

weeklyPatterns.notes: Recovery week — every 3-4 weeks. B2B replaced with single shorter long run. Reduced intensity.

taper.notes: CTS Ultra taper: longer and gentler than road taper. 70% / 50% / 30% volume across 3 weeks. For 100-milers, often extends to 4 weeks.

strengthRecommendation.philosophy: Koop strongly recommends strength training for ultrarunners — single-leg work, hip/glute strength, core stability, posterior chain. 2× per week, 30-45 min sessions. Critical for durability and injury prevention given high training loads.

crossTrainingRecommendation.intensityGuidance: Hiking is the most race-specific cross-training for mountain ultras — counts toward both training stimulus and durability. Cycling is acceptable for aerobic supplementation on rest days. Easy effort only.

restrictions.rule: Built specifically for ultras (50K and beyond). Not designed for road races up to the marathon — overly long training sessions and insufficient pace specificity for shorter races.
restrictions.warningMessage: CTS Ultra is built for ultras. For road marathon, consider Pfitzinger or Daniels — they're more pace-specific.

restrictions.rule: Requires substantial running base (50+ miles per week or equivalent training time) and prior race experience. Not appropriate for first-time ultrarunners without a coaching relationship.
restrictions.warningMessage: CTS Ultra plans assume serious training history. For first-time ultrarunners, Roche/SWAP is more accessible and emphasizes joy/play over volume.

restrictions.rule: Plans require 8-20 hours/week and access to trails (or hills) for terrain specificity. Hard for runners without trail access or limited weekly time.
restrictions.warningMessage: CTS Ultra requires significant weekly time and ideally trail/hill access. With limited time or road-only access, results will be compromised — but the system can be adapted with cycling/hiking substitutes.

invariants: Long run cap at 45% of weekly mileage (looser than road methods due to ultra demands)
Back-to-back long runs only in specific_prep and race_prep phases
B2B Day 2 must be 50-70% of B2B Day 1 duration
Vertical gain progression: track weekly elevation gain alongside mileage for mountain races
ClimbingRepeats only when user has hasHillsNearby = true
Hiking counts as training time (especially Z2 vertical-gain hikes)
If user lacks trail access, substitute road hill repeats but warn that race specificity is reduced
